title: Campus Ride
summary: Student-to-student rides for Livingstone, where riders name their own price.

meta.label: TIMELINE
meta.value: v1: September 2026. Audit, fixes, and expansion: Oct 3 to 9, 2026.

blocks.text: Getting off campus without a car is hard. A grocery run, a doctor’s appointment, or a trip to the pharmacy can mean asking around in group chats and hoping someone is free.
Meanwhile plenty of students with cars would happily drive a classmate for a few dollars. The two groups just do not have a simple, trusted way to find each other.
Campus Ride connects them: verified Livingstone students, riding with and driving for each other, at a price the rider proposes.

Salisbury is hard to get around without a car. The trips students need most are groceries, the pharmacy, and getting to the bus or train station before breaks. Today that means asking in group chats and hoping someone answers. I wanted asking for a ride to feel less like asking for a favor.
Campus Ride covers both sides of a trip, from booking a ride to getting paid for driving one.

blocks.caption: 12 seconds. A rider sets a destination and a price, driver offers come in, and the rider accepts one.
Booking flow: home, destination, set your price, schedule a ride, finding a driver, driver offers, and no drivers available.

blocks.text: Riders verify as students, pick a destination, set a price, and choose from driver offers. Drivers apply with a student ID and their documents, go online, and get requests with a countdown. Both sides have the unhappy screens too: no internet, payment failed, no drivers available. It comes to 76 mobile screens in 13 flows, and a clickable prototype.

blocks.title: Riders name the price, with a suggestion

blocks.text: Fixed prices are simple but feel wrong between classmates on tight budgets. Fully open pricing is fair but slow, and nobody knows what is reasonable.

So the "Set your price" step shows a suggested price ($7.00) next to an offer the rider can change ($6.00). The suggestion starts from distance and estimated drive time. It gives people a starting point, and the offer keeps them in control.

It took five versions of the destination screen to get here, moving the map and the destination list around. In the end I stopped asking one screen to do everything. Choosing where you are going and agreeing on a price are different decisions, so each got its own screen.

blocks.caption: Five versions of the destination screen.

blocks.title: I audited my first 11 screens before adding any new ones

blocks.text: My first 11 screens were a solid happy path. The fast move was to keep adding. But every problem in those 11 would get copied into the next 65.

items.text: Two type families and 18 text sizes, some fractional, like 11.545 px.
The primary button existed in five sizes and radii.
Two chips came in under 3:1 contrast, and input borders were 1.48:1.
Tap targets as small as 16 px, and copy slips like "Kannaplois" and "Salibury."

blocks.text: I fixed the foundation first: one type scale, every color bound to a variable, a radius scale, 44 px hit areas, and one price format. Then I turned the repeating patterns into components, starting with Button, Input, Header, Stepper, and Bottom sheet.

blocks.caption: Driver offers, before and after the audit.

blocks.text: A marketplace has a lot of screens that look alike. If the base pieces are consistent, every new screen is faster to make and easier to trust.

blocks.title: Design the negotiation on both sides, including when it fails

blocks.text: Name your price only works if drivers can respond and riders can choose. And it has to handle the awkward moments: nobody accepts, or a driver loses out.

steps.title: Riders see driver offers
steps.text: Each has a verified badge, rating, ETA, and price. One is tagged Best Match.

steps.title: Drivers get a request with a countdown
steps.text: They can accept, decline, or counter, and see what they take home after the fee.

steps.title: When no one accepts
steps.text: The rider gets "No drivers available" and two ways forward: raise the offer or schedule for later.

steps.title: Drivers get closure too
steps.text: "Rider chose someone else" and "You missed a request" explain what happened.

frame.caption: The offer loop: driver offers, counter offer, and no drivers available.

blocks.text: The numbers in these screens, like typical offer ranges and the 10% fee, are placeholder copy, not real data. I would set the real fee after asking drivers what feels fair.
A marketplace is only as good as its worst moment. If a rider’s offer is too low, the app should help them fix it, not leave them waiting.

items.title: Audit before you scale.
items.text: Fixing 11 screens was cheap. Fixing 76 would not have been.

items.title: Split, do not squeeze.
items.text: When a screen keeps getting rearranged, it might be two screens.

items.title: Two-sided means twice the empathy.
items.text: Designing "Rider chose someone else" made me care about how the app feels for the person who loses out, not just the person who wins.

blocks.text: Campus Ride has not launched, so there are no users or metrics yet. What I most want to learn is whether a rider’s first offer gets accepted, and how many students would sign up to drive. A short survey in student group chats and through ColorStack could answer the second one before I build anything.

items.text: Talk to ten students: five who need rides and five who have cars.
Settle the safety and verification rules: student email, student ID, and driver documents.
Test the offer loop in the prototype with real classmates.
